title: How to add CSS
summary: Covers the three ways to attach CSS to HTML: inline (style attribute), internal (<style> element) and external (separate .css file connected with <link>). Explains the anatomy of a CSS rule and when each method fits, then an exercise builds a four-page site that uses all three methods.

concepts.heading: The three methods at a glance
points: Inline: CSS written in a style attribute on one element. Affects only that element.
Internal: CSS written inside a <style> element in the HTML file. Affects only that one HTML page.
External: CSS written in a separate file with a .css extension (often style.css, styles.css or main.css), connected to each page with a <link> element. Affects every page that links to it.

Rule of thumb from the lecture: inline for a single element, internal for a single page, external for a multi-page site (and for most real work). External is the method used for the rest of the course; the other two are still worth recognising because they show up in other people's code.

concepts.heading: Inline CSS: the style attribute
points: style is a global attribute: it can go on any element (html, img, br, h1, anything).
It follows the usual attribute pattern: name, equals sign, then a value in quotes. The value is the CSS.

Inside the value, a declaration has two parts: the property to change and the value to set it to, separated by a colon and ended with a semicolon. Example: style="background: blue;" on the <html> opening tag makes the whole page background blue.
Inline CSS always goes in the opening tag of the element being styled.

Downside: to give many elements the same look you must repeat the attribute on every one, which is tedious and hard to maintain. Use it sparingly: for one-off tweaks, a single element, or quick testing.

concepts.heading: Internal CSS: the <style> element
points: Open a <style> tag and close it with </style>; everything between them is CSS.
Because a <style> block can affect any element in the document, each rule needs a selector to say which elements it targets. Inline CSS doesn't need one because it already sits on the target element.

Rule anatomy: selector, then an opening curly brace, then one or more property: value; declarations, then a closing curly brace. It is usually spread over several lines for readability, but it is the same as writing it on one line: html { background: red; }
One <style> block can hold as many rules as needed, targeting as many different elements as needed.
Convention: put the <style> element inside <head>. The browser will still apply it if it's placed elsewhere, but developers keep it in the head.
Limitation: the rules only apply to the page that contains them, so internal CSS doesn't suit multi-page sites.

concepts.heading: External CSS: a .css file plus <link>
points: The CSS lives in its own file. That file contains only rules (selectors, properties, values), with no HTML tags and no <style> wrapper.
Connect it from inside the HTML page's <head> with a <link> element. <link> is a void (self-closing) element: no closing tag.
rel (relationship) says what role the linked file plays for this page. For CSS it is rel="stylesheet".
href says where the file is. ./style.css means 'style.css in the same folder as this HTML file'.
Every page that links the same file gets the same styles, so one edit restyles the whole site. This is why external CSS is the standard approach.

concepts.heading: Revision used in the exercise: links and relative paths
points: Links between pages are anchor elements: Inline.
./ means 'start from the current folder', then the filename follows the forward slash.
The Solution folder holds a second copy of every file. Preview solution.html to see the target, then collapse that folder in VS Code so the duplicate filenames don't get mixed up.

code_examples.caption: Inline: style attribute in the opening tag (here on <html> to colour the whole page)
Internal: a <style> block in the head with a selector and curly braces
External: link the stylesheet in the head; the .css file holds only rules
code_examples.code:
<!-- index.html -->
<head>
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="./styles.css" />
</head>

/* styles.css */
html {
  background: green;
}

task.name: 5.1 Adding CSS: three methods, four pages
task.starting_point: A project folder with five files: index.html (an h1 'Three Methods of Adding CSS' and a comment asking for three links), inline.html, internal.html and external.html (each with an h1 telling you what colour and method to use), and an empty style.css. A Solution folder holds the finished versions.
task.goal: Turn index.html into a home page that links to the three other pages, then colour each page's h1 using the method that page is named after: blue with inline, red with internal, green with external.
steps: In index.html, under the h1, add three anchor tags whose href values are ./inline.html, ./internal.html and ./external.html, with link text Inline, Internal, External.
In inline.html, add style="color: blue" to the opening <h1> tag.
In internal.html, add a <style> element inside <head> containing a rule that selects h1 and sets color: red.
In style.css, write a rule that selects h1 and sets color: green.
In external.html, add <link rel="stylesheet" href="./style.css" /> inside <head> so the page loads style.css.
Preview index.html, click each link and check each h1 is the right colour. Compare with Solution/solution.html.
task.expected_result: A home page with the heading and three working links. The Inline page shows a blue h1 ('Style Me in Blue!'), the Internal page a red one, and the External page a green one.

solution_code.code:
Three Methods of Adding CSS

Inline Internal External

Style Me in Blue!

/* style.css */ h1 { color: green; }

pitfalls: Writing a selector and braces inside a style attribute. Inline CSS is just property: value pairs.
Forgetting the selector or curly braces inside <style> or a .css file.
Putting <style> tags inside the .css file. External files contain only CSS rules.
Wrong href in <link> (wrong filename, e.g. styles.css vs style.css, or wrong folder), so the stylesheet silently never loads.
Leaving out rel="stylesheet"; the browser then doesn't treat the file as CSS.
Adding a closing </link> tag. It is a void element.
Editing the copy in the Solution folder by mistake because it has the same filenames.

playground.coverage: Covers all three methods with matching colours (inline blue, internal red, external green), uses the CSS pane as the external stylesheet, and has a 'Which one wins?' explore demo plus a notes table with the <link> syntax and what rel/href mean.
gaps_and_ideas: The course exercise is a 4-page site (home page linking to inline/internal/external pages) that also revises anchors and ./ relative paths. The playground squeezes it into one page with three h2s, so that revision is lost. Consider a task that adds the three links, or a note explaining the change.

The internal-style solution uses a class selector (.internal), but classes are only taught in the next lecture; the course uses the element selector h1. Either switch to a selector learners already know, or add a one-line hint about what .internal means.
Add a 'rule anatomy' diagram (selector, curly braces, property, colon, value, semicolon) and the comparison that inline CSS has no selector because it is already on the element.
Mention that style is a global attribute (works on any element, e.g. <html style="background: blue"> to colour the whole page), matching the lecture's slides.
Add the convention that <style> and <link> go inside <head>, and that <link> is self-closing.
Explore demo idea: a 'multi-page' toggle showing two mini pages sharing one external stylesheet; edit the shared CSS once and both update, versus internal CSS where only one page changes.
